The decision to keep or shorten the tea-serving ceremony depends on several factors, including cultural traditions, the size of the family, the overall wedding schedule, and the couple’s vision for the event. Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **Answer: 1 (You are not in the wrong.)** ### **Why?** Your decision to refuse the loan is **completely reasonable**—and even responsible—given the circumstances. Here’s why: #### **1. It’s Your Money, Your Goals** - You’ve been **consciously saving** for **your own dream** (a post-graduation vacation) for years. That’s a **personal achievement**, not something you owe to your brother. - You’re in **business school**, which is expensive and stressful—this fund is likely your **only real reward** for all your hard work. Taking it away would be **self-sabotaging**. - Even if he *could* pay you back, **life happens** (job loss, emergencies, poor planning). You’re not a bank. #### **2. He’s a Poor Financial Steward** - You’ve **documented his bad habits** (always broke, never saves, relies on parents). Borrowing from you would just **perpetuate the cycle**. - His argument that he’s been "working harder" (college/job) is **flawed**—you’re both adults now, and his choices (moving back in, not budgeting) are his responsibility. - If he *really* wanted to save, he could have done so **without relying on you or parents**. Now he’s asking for a **handout**, not a loan. #### **3. His Entitlement is Unjustified** - **"Mom and Dad spoiled me"** is **backwards logic**. If anything, your parents **spoiled him** by enabling his financial irresponsibility (letting him live rent-free, covering bills, etc.). - **"I got to go on trips more"** is **not a debt**. You’re not obligated to fund his leisure because you had privileges in the past. - **"I had to go back to school"** is **not an excuse**. He could have **budgeted differently**—this isn’t a "sacrifice" that deserves compensation. #### **4. The Emotional & Practical Risks** - **He’ll likely not pay you back on time** (or at all). Even if he *intends* to, his track record suggests otherwise. - **You’ll resent him** if you do this, and resentment destroys relationships. - **You’ll resent yourself** for enabling his bad habits, which could affect your own financial discipline. ### **What You Could Do Instead:** ✅ **Set firm boundaries** – *"No, I’m not lending you money. If you want to save for a trip, you’ll have to do it yourself."* ✅ **Offer alternatives** – *"If you really want to go to Japan, maybe we can plan a trip together when I graduate?"* (But don’t fund it.) ✅ **Document the conversation** – If he keeps pressuring you, write down your refusal and move on. ✅ **Protect your fund** – If he keeps asking, **freeze the money in a separate account** (even if it’s just a savings note) so he can’t guilt-trip you. ### **Final Verdict:** You are **not** in the wrong. **You are being fair to yourself, responsible with your money, and setting a boundary that protects your future.** His reaction is **childish and entitled**, not justified. Would you like help drafting a response to him? Sometimes a **polite but firm** message can shut down the guilt-tripping.
